name: Hassan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hassan. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We don't work for companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee on a hydraulic excavator at Tallow Creek, the big gold pit. Basically I sit in a cab the size of a small kitchen and load haul trucks, four passes per truck if you're good, five or six if you're me. Twelve-hour shifts, rotating days and nights. I love the machine, honestly, it's like the biggest toy in the world. What wears me out is nights, and the trainer, Bev, sighing when I miss the truck bed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on an excavator?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drove a forklift at the port warehouse for twenty-five years. Then they brought in robot carts that move the pallets themselves, and at fifty-five I was out, along with forty others. I'd already been watching videos about mining equipment, so I applied here the same month. My wife Leila had surgery last year and our son's food truck went under, and we helped with both, so our savings are basically gone, a few weeks at most. But I'd do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, alright, so it's a tool, like a good calculator. I'd probably post something on the miners' forum I follow, asking what the AI tools are actually good for then. I'm the guy who wants to know how things work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, really. I'd keep using AI the way I do now, to quiz myself on the safety rules and plan my shopping. If AI stays a tool, I'll just be the old man who's weirdly good with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the excavator and try to get signed off as a full operator within the year. I'd keep using the AI to study the machine manuals. And I'd start putting a little away again now that the medical bills are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by it, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you use AI every day. What does that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it things on my break, like why the hydraulics feel slow when it's cold, and it explains it better than the manual. I record a voice note after shift about what went wrong and ask it for tips. Bev thinks I'm crazy, but my passes are getting quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After the port, does a quiet plateau feel safe to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer, not safe. The port taught me that the robot doesn't need to be clever, just cheaper. The carts that replaced us were stupid machines, really. So I'd still keep my eyes open.

S0.say: He'd say AI is just a tool, like a good calculator, and ask on a miners' forum what AI tools are actually good for.
S0.think: He thinks a plateau changes nothing for him: he'd keep using AI to study and plan, and be the older worker who's unusually good with it.
S0.do: Keeps working toward full sign-off on the excavator within a year, using AI to study the manuals. Starts saving again now that the medical bills are paid.
S0.quote: If AI stays a tool, I'll just be the old man who's weirdly good with it.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan has already lost a job to automation and still talks about machines with affection. He uses AI daily in practical ways, recording voice notes after shift to improve. His lesson from the port, that cheap robots don't need to be clever, keeps him watchful even in the calmest picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to happen whether we like it or not, so let's be the ones who learn it. At work I'd tell the guys not to wait. I wouldn't blame the robots, I'd blame companies that don't plan for their people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've done this once already, so I'm not as scared as the others. At the port I was angry for a week, then I watched mining videos for a month, then I had a new job. I think I can do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company about the remote operations centre in the first week and sign up for any course. I'd use AI to learn the basics of automation systems in the evenings. If Tallow Creek wasn't training people, I'd look at the other mines that are, even if it means driving further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it risky, with almost no savings, to be the first to jump?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Leila reminds me. But the risk at the port was not jumping. The guys who waited for the company to look after them were the ones still looking for work two years later. With little money you can't afford to be slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, actually, my trainer. She's sixty, brilliant on the machine, but she won't touch a computer. She's taught me everything and she'd be the one left behind. I'd try to drag her to the course with me.

S1.say: He'd tell co-workers not to wait but to be the ones who learn the new systems, blaming companies that don't plan for their people rather than the robots.
S1.think: He thinks he's less scared than others because he's already rebuilt his working life once, after the port, and believes he can do it again.
S1.do: Asks about the remote operations centre in the first week and signs up for any course, studying automation basics with AI in the evenings. Looks at other mines that train people if his own doesn't, even with a longer drive.
S1.quote: At the port I was angry for a week, then I watched mining videos for a month, then I had a new job.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan's calm comes from experience, not money; he has almost no savings and admits it's risky. His point that thin savings make waiting more dangerous is a neat reversal of what one might expect. He worries most for his trainer Bev, a skilled operator who refuses computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to move fast, and companies too, because two years is no time. I'd say, everybody learn what you can, help each other. I wouldn't panic in public, it doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one is different from the port. At the port there was another industry to run to. If robots do everything in two years, where do I run? I'd be sixty with a few weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for every course they offered in the first month, remote ops, maintenance, anything, and use AI to cram. We'd cut the car and the extras and live on Leila's part-time wage if we had to. And I'd look for jobs setting up or fixing the new robots, because someone has to, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Under pressure, but I'd still feel I could move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said yourself there might be nowhere to run. Isn't that a contradiction with signing up for everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is. But sitting still is worse for me than running in the wrong direction. If I'm going to lose, I'd rather lose while trying. That's just how I'm made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leila and your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leila we've started from nothing before, after the port, and we'll do it again. I'd tell my son to come with me to the robot jobs, he's thirty and he knows engines from the food truck. Maybe we'd do it together.

S2.say: He'd say government and companies must move fast and that everyone should learn what they can and help each other, while avoiding public panic.
S2.think: He thinks this is different from the port because there'd be no other industry to run to, and at sixty he'd have only a few weeks of money.
S2.do: Signs up for every course in the first month and crams with AI. Cuts the car and extras, living on his wife's part-time wage if needed, and hunts for jobs installing or fixing the new robots.
S2.feel: Anxious and under pressure, but still able to move.
S2.quote: At the port there was another industry to run to. If robots do everything in two years, where do I run?
S2.fieldNote: This is the first picture where Hassan's port experience stops reassuring him, and he names why. When the contradiction was put to him, he accepted it calmly: he'd rather lose while trying. He'd bring his son into the robot work with him, which shows how he turns worry into a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell people at the pit to learn, plan and stop arguing about whether it's real. Online I'd share any free courses I found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me sixty-three. Five years is long enough for me to become the guy who fixes the robot excavator instead of the guy it replaces. I really think I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the two-year technical diploma in mechatronics at night, robots plus mechanics, with AI as my tutor. I'd save a bit every month, now the bills are paid, so we have three months put by before it arrives. And I'd still go for full operator sign-off, because that's pay right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A diploma, full sign-off and saving, all at once. Where does the time come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the nights I spend watching videos anyway. I'd swap the videos for the course. My days off would go, and Leila wouldn't be thrilled, but it's two years of hard work for maybe ten years of work after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they won't hire a sixty-three-year-old technician, even with the paper. Companies say they value experience, then they hire the twenty-five-year-old. That's the part I can't control.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, tell colleagues to stop arguing about whether it's real, and share free courses online.
S3.think: He believes five years is long enough to become the person who repairs the robot excavator rather than the one it replaces.
S3.do: Studies for a two-year night diploma in mechatronics with AI as his tutor. Saves monthly to build three months of cushion and keeps working toward full operator sign-off.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to become the guy who fixes the robot excavator instead of the guy it replaces.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Hassan's energy into a clear plan, though he is aware that employers may not hire an older technician. He is willing to give up his days off for it. His worry is about age discrimination, not his own ability to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. I'd tell the young guys to take every course going. I'd probably start a little group at the pit to share what we're learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me sixty-eight, so I'd probably retire about when it arrives. With ten years I could actually enjoy learning the robots instead of running from them. That's a nice thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mechatronics diploma at a normal pace and try to move into maintenance by year five. We'd build some savings, maybe six months by the end. And I'd run that learning group, using AI to make the materials simple for guys who hate reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-eight, or keep going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Depends on the money. With a small pension and some savings, I'd retire but maybe do a few hours training people. I don't like sitting still. Leila wants to visit her sister abroad, so maybe that first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Bev come to your learning group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I bribed her with doughnuts, maybe. Ten years is long enough even for Bev to change her mind. She'd say she won't, then she'd come and argue with everything, which would make it better.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift, tell younger workers to take every course, and start a learning group at the pit.
S4.think: He thinks he'd likely retire around when AGI arrives at sixty-eight, and could enjoy learning the robots rather than running from them.
S4.do: Completes the mechatronics diploma at a normal pace, aiming to move into maintenance by year five. Builds about six months of savings and runs a learning group, using AI to simplify materials.
S4.quote: With ten years I could actually enjoy learning the robots instead of running from them.
S4.fieldNote: Hassan is at ease with a decade's warning, and his instinct is to help others learn. He's realistic that retirement depends on money and would keep doing some training work. His affection for Bev comes through again, and he expects even her to come round.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's nowhere to run and no time to learn. What would help is paid training that starts the day the news hits, open to older workers too, and some money to live on while you learn. And companies that hire the older guys once we've done the training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask what people like me learned the first time. The robot carts at the port weren't smart. They were cheap and they didn't need lunch, and that was enough. People think it's about clever AI, but cheap is usually enough.

headlineQuote: The robot carts at the port weren't smart. They were cheap and they didn't need lunch, and that was enough.
portrait: Hassan Fischer is 58 and a trainee excavator operator at the Tallow Creek gold pit, a job he took at fifty-five after robot carts replaced him and forty others at a port warehouse. Medical bills and his son's failed food truck have used up his savings, but he loves machines and uses AI every day to learn. Having rebuilt his working life once, he is calm in a plateau and in steady disruption. The two-year picture makes him anxious because there'd be nowhere to run, though he'd still sign up for every course. With five or ten years he plans a night diploma in mechatronics and hopes to fix the robots rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no other industry to run to and no time to learn something new.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training from the day the news breaks, open to older workers with money to live on while learning, and companies willing to hire older people afterwards.
